transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. Lee. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Lee. Um, thank you for seeing me. So, I guess the reason I'm here is—well, it’s been a really overwhelming couple of weeks, to be honest. 

Basically, I just moved into a new apartment, and for a while, I was barely even settling in. I mean, there were cardboard boxes stacked to the ceiling in the living room, I hadn’t even unpacked my kitchen, and I hadn't properly set up my home office, which is a huge deal for me since I’m a digital interface designer and I really need my workspace to be functional. I was just kind of existing around the mess. 

But then, I don't know, it was like a switch just completely flipped in my brain. I went from doing absolutely nothing to suddenly taking on, well, everything. I started saying yes to all these mentoring sessions for junior designers, which I usually never have the bandwidth for because it takes so much prep time. And then I started taking on all these extra client prototypes at work—like, really complex, interactive wireframes that take hours and hours to build out. I just kept telling people, "Yeah, send it over, I can do it." 

And if that wasn't enough, right in the middle of all these extra projects and living out of half-empty boxes, I decided I absolutely had to redesign my entire professional portfolio from scratch. The layout, the case studies, the UI components, all of it. It honestly felt like I had to fix my entire life, my whole career, in just one giant sprint. Like if I didn't get it all done perfectly right in that exact moment, I was failing. I just kept adding and adding to my plate, and... yeah, it's just been a lot, and I realized I probably needed to talk to someone about why I keep doing this to myself.
During these past couple of weeks when you were taking on all these projects, did you notice you needed much less sleep than usual, yet still felt full of energy?

Oh, wow, yes. Yes, exactly that. It's actually really strange when you put it like that, but yes. I mean, usually, I'm the kind of person who absolutely needs a solid seven or eight hours of sleep, especially because looking at screens all day and doing pixel-perfect design work just completely drains my eyes and my brain. If I don't sleep normally, I get these terrible tension headaches right behind my temples. 

But during this whole... whatever this was over the last couple of weeks, sleep just felt like this completely unnecessary interruption. Like, it actually felt like a waste of time. I remember for several nights in a row, I was staying up until maybe 2:00 or 3:00 in the morning, tweaking the CSS on my portfolio or writing out these incredibly long, detailed feedback emails for the junior designers I was mentoring. And then I'd be wide awake by 6:00 or 6:30 AM. So I was getting, what, maybe three or four hours of sleep? Tops? 

And the craziest part is, I didn't feel tired at all. Normally, if I sleep three hours, I'm a zombie. I can't even make coffee without spilling it. But I would wake up before my alarm even went off, and my brain was already going a million miles an hour. I'd just lay there in the dark for a second, and then I’d be completely convinced that I was totally fine, completely rested, and that I should just get up and use the extra time to get ahead on my wireframes before the rest of the team logged on. I was just buzzing with all this energy, like I was plugged straight into a wall socket. I didn't even need caffeine, which is saying something for me. It was just... go, go, go, from the second I opened my eyes.
Before these past couple of weeks, have you ever had episodes—lasting a week or more—where you felt persistently sad, low on energy, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah... yeah, actually. That's—that's kind of the whole reason the apartment was in such a state with all those boxes in the first place, before I went into that weird overdrive. Before that, for... gosh, a really long time, I was just so incredibly down. 

It’s hard to even explain how deep it goes, but lately, or I guess right up until that switch flipped, I would wake up with this... this really heavy, just completely gray feeling right in the center of my chest. It literally feels like a physical weight, you know? Like someone poured wet concrete into my ribs while I was sleeping. I’d just lie there in bed staring at the ceiling, feeling completely paralyzed by it. 

And the worst part is, it doesn't even make sense. Like, the apartment would be totally quiet, absolutely nothing bad is happening in my life—my job is fine, I just moved to this new place—but I would just feel this overwhelming, crushing sadness. I remember walking into the kitchen one morning, and I saw a dirty coffee mug sitting in the sink. Just a normal, everyday mug that I hadn't washed. And I just stared at it, and I felt like I could just completely break down and cry over it. Over a coffee mug! 

It’s like every tiny little thing is just insurmountable, and that heavy, gray feeling just taints everything I look at. It makes me feel like I can't even participate in my own life, let alone do my design work or talk to my friends or even just unpack my clothes. It's just so exhausting to feel that way day after day, walking around like you're underwater, where even the absolute smallest things just feel like climbing a mountain, and you just can't figure out why you can't snap out of it...
During that high-energy period, did you ever experience anything like hearing voices, seeing things that others didn't, or having beliefs that seemed unusual or that others said weren't true?

Oh, no, definitely not. Nothing like that. I mean, I know sometimes when people get really, really sleep-deprived, their brains can start playing tricks on them, but I never experienced anything where I was hearing voices or seeing things that weren't actually in the room. 

My thoughts were incredibly loud, if that makes sense? But it was always just my own voice. Just my own normal inner monologue, except instead of talking at a regular pace, it was like someone had put it on 2x or 3x speed—like when you listen to an audiobook and you just want to get through it faster. But it was always just me, thinking about my projects, or CSS coding, or whether I should use a specific sans-serif font for a client's landing page. It was all very grounded in reality, just... a very, very sped-up version of my normal reality. 

And as for the beliefs thing... I mean, I guess you could say I was maybe overly optimistic about how much I could physically accomplish in a 24-hour period? Like, my friend Jess actually came over during that second week to drop off some Thai takeout because she knew I wasn't cooking with the kitchen still completely packed up in those boxes. And she told me I was being completely unrealistic, thinking I could mentor three junior designers, do my day job, take on extra prototypes, and rebuild my entire professional portfolio from scratch all at the same time. She kept saying, "You're not superhuman, you can't do all this." 

But it’s not like I actually believed I was superhuman or had magical powers or anything bizarre like that. I didn't have any strange delusions. I just genuinely felt like I had finally cracked the code on time management and workflow efficiency. I just felt incredibly capable, you know? Like I was finally functioning at my absolute peak potential and everyone else was just moving too slow to see it. But I always knew exactly who I was, where I was, and what I was doing. I definitely wasn't seeing or hearing anything strange. It was really just... me, dialed up to an absolute hundred.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a distinct manic episode lasting at least two weeks characterized by decreased need for sleep, increased energy, grandiosity/overconfidence, pressured/racing thoughts, and excessive involvement in goal-directed activities (mentoring, extra client work, portfolio redesign) causing impaired judgment and functional overcommitment, without hallucinations or delusions. This follows a preceding major depressive episode with depressed mood, anhedonia, low energy, and feelings of worthlessness lasting weeks. The presence of both a manic and depressive episode establishes Bipolar I Disorder; absence of psychotic features during the manic episode specifies the 'without psychotic symptoms' subtype (F31.1), differentiating from F31.2 (with psychotic features) and F30.1 (single manic episode without prior depressive episode, which does not apply here given clear history of prior depression).
